title: Holding Things in Mind
objective: After this level you can explain working memory's small capacity and how chunking stretches it.
summary: Working memory holds the few thoughts you are using right now. Miller put its limit at seven, plus or minus two; later research says about four chunks, and chunking packs more into each one.

cards.headline: Try holding 5205550467 in your head. Now try 520-555-0467.
cards.body: Same ten digits, yet the second version feels far easier to keep. Nothing about the numbers changed. What changed is how many things your mind has to juggle at once.

cards.headline: Working memory: the mind's workbench
cards.body: Short-term memory is best seen as one part of working memory: the few thoughts you're actively holding and using right now. You lean on it when you carry a digit in mental arithmetic, keep the start of a sentence in mind until it ends, or plan the order of your errands. It's where thinking happens, and the bench is surprisingly small.

cards.headline: Seven, then four
cards.body: In 1956, George Miller reviewed the research on short-term memory and found people can hold between 5 and 9 items. He called it "the magical number seven, plus or minus two." Later research revised it downward. When people can't rehearse or group items, young adults hold only about 3 to 5 chunks, and researchers led by Nelson Cowan now put working memory's capacity at about 4.

cards.headline: Chunking: packing more into each slot
cards.body: The limit counts chunks, not raw items. A chunk is any group your mind treats as one unit, so 520-555-0467 is three chunks, not ten digits. In Cowan's studies, word pairs people had learned together, like desk-ball, took up one slot, the same as a single word. Need bread, milk and pepper? Picture bread floating in peppery milk, and three items become one.

cards.headline: Holding things in mind
learned: Working memory holds the few thoughts in use right now
Miller (1956): seven, plus or minus two
Chunking packs several items into one unit

questions.prompt: Which capacity for short-term memory did George Miller's 1956 review make famous?

options.label: Two items, plus or minus one
options.rationale: Far too low: Miller found people held 5 to 9 items.

options.label: Four chunks, plus or minus one
options.rationale: That's the later revision by Cowan and others, not Miller's number.

options.label: Seven items, plus or minus two
Twelve items, plus or minus three
options.rationale: Too high: Miller's range topped out at 9 items.

questions.explanation: Miller found people hold between 5 and 9 items and called it "the magical number seven, plus or minus two." Later research revised it to about four chunks.

questions.prompt: How does chunking let you hold more in working memory?

options.label: It makes working memory physically bigger
options.rationale: The limit stays about the same; chunking changes what fills each slot.

options.label: It groups items into units that each fill one slot
It sends the items straight to sensory memory
options.rationale: Sensory memory lasts only seconds and isn't where you work with information.

options.label: It removes the need to pay attention
options.rationale: Chunking is an active strategy, not a way to skip attention.

questions.explanation: The limit counts chunks, not items. Grouping several items into one meaningful unit lets each slot hold more.

questions.prompt: Level 31's short-term memory, which lasts about 15 to 30 seconds, is best seen as one part of which larger system?

options.label: Sensory memory
options.rationale: Sensory memory is the stop before short-term memory, not a larger system around it.

options.label: Long-term memory
options.rationale: Long-term memory is where rehearsed information goes next.

options.label: The forgetting curve
options.rationale: That's a pattern of forgetting, not a memory system.

questions.explanation: Short-term memory is one component of working memory, the few thoughts you actively hold and use.
